stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO
stories.move: Nvidia's board said Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO and a board member, effective immediately. The move follows a board investigation opened Nov. 8 after Huang disclosed a relationship with an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. intelligence has linked to Beijing; the New York Times reported Nov. 11 that Huang had a separate relationship with an Nvidia vice president who reported to him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO while keeping her CFO title, and former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones became Nvidia's first-ever board chair. Shares fell 4.3% Thursday after swinging as much as 14% intraday, closing just above a $4 trillion market cap.
stories.why: It's a sudden end for the executive most identified with the AI boom, days before Nvidia's next earnings report and a planned closed-door briefing for House committees on his conduct.
stories.bear: No permanent successor has been named, and a rushed leadership change this close to earnings could unsettle customers mid-cycle in the AI buildout.
stories.watch: Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter results Nov. 17 and the board's search for a permanent CEO.

stories.headline: Alphabet discloses new $548 million Qualcomm stake
stories.move: Alphabet's third-quarter 13F, filed Nov. 6 for holdings as of Sept. 30, showed a new position of about 2.98 million Qualcomm shares worth roughly $548 million. Its stake in SpaceX grew to about 555 million shares worth $83.7 billion, nearly 95% of the disclosed portfolio.
stories.why: The Qualcomm stake is a rare new addition to Alphabet's public stock filing as AI infrastructure spending accelerates, and the SpaceX position shows how dominant that single holding remains in Alphabet's outside portfolio.
stories.bear: A 13F only shows U.S.-listed stock positions at quarter-end; it doesn't explain why the Qualcomm shares were bought or whether the position has changed since.
stories.watch: Alphabet's next 13F, due by mid-February, for whether the Qualcomm stake grows.

stories.headline: AMD jumps on Google Cloud deal, analyst upgrade
stories.move: AMD said Nov. 9 its fifth-generation EPYC server chips will host Google Cloud's new TPU 8tx system, the first cloud TPU built with hardware-level encryption for secure AI computing. The same day, Oppenheimer upgraded AMD to Outperform from Perform with a $600 price target, citing AMD's data-center growth. Shares rose about 12%.
stories.why: The Google deal extends AMD's AI business beyond its own chips into the hardware that hosts a rival's cloud systems, and Oppenheimer's upgrade projects AMD's data-center revenue growing about 135% in 2027.
stories.bear: AMD didn't disclose pricing, availability or independent performance benchmarks for the new Google system, and the stock's 12% jump already prices in much of that projected growth.
stories.watch: AMD's next quarterly report for whether data-center revenue growth tracks Oppenheimer's forecast.

Several large investors' third-quarter 13F filings are due by Nov. 16, including Berkshire Hathaway, Citadel, Appaloosa and the Gates Foundation Trust.
Walmart reports fiscal third-quarter results Nov. 19.
memo: A CEO's personal conduct can erase tens of billions in market value within days; have a succession plan ready before a crisis forces one.
When a company discloses a new stake in a supplier to its rivals, it's often a signal about where it sees the next bottleneck in its own industry.
A single analyst upgrade tied to a named customer deal can move a stock more than a strong earnings report; markets reward concrete proof over guidance.
